reference.source: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics / Ashcraft Pediatric Surgery
clinicalPearls: Congenital interruption of the intestinal lumen producing neonatal obstruction, most commonly in the jejunum and ileum and less often in the colon
Jejunoileal atresia is largely attributed to a late intrauterine mesenteric vascular accident rather than a primary failure of recanalisation
The more distal the atresia, the greater the number of dilated loops and air-fluid levels; proximal jejunal atresia gives few dilated loops
Classified into types I (membrane), II (fibrous cord), IIIa (V-shaped mesenteric gap), IIIb (apple-peel/Christmas-tree), and IV (multiple atresias)
The apple-peel (type IIIb) variant features a proximal atresia with the distal bowel coiled around a single perfusing vessel and carries higher morbidity
Bilious vomiting, abdominal distension, and failure to pass meconium in a neonate should prompt urgent evaluation for atresia
Treatment is surgical resection of the atretic segment with primary anastomosis, often tapering the dilated proximal bowel to restore peristalsis
reference.pathophysiology: Jejunoileal atresia is thought to result from a localised intrauterine mesenteric vascular insult (for example volvulus, intussusception, or a strangulated segment) that devitalises a portion of already-formed bowel, which is then resorbed, leaving an atretic gap and a variable mesenteric defect. This contrasts with duodenal atresia, which reflects failed recanalisation of the solid embryonic cord. The proximal bowel becomes dilated, hypertrophied, and dysmotile, while the distal bowel is small and unused. Colonic atresia is rarer and follows a similar vascular mechanism. Extensive or apple-peel patterns may leave a foreshortened bowel and predispose to short-bowel syndrome.
additionalDifferentials: Meconium plug syndrome or small left colon
additionalInvestigations: Abdominal radiograph to count dilated loops and gauge the level of obstruction
Water-soluble contrast enema to assess a microcolon and exclude colonic atresia or meconium ileus
Upper gastrointestinal contrast study when malrotation cannot be excluded
Prenatal ultrasound review for dilated bowel loops and polyhydramnios
Screening for cystic fibrosis given overlap with meconium ileus
Assessment of bowel length at operation to anticipate short-bowel risk
redFlags: Bilious vomiting in a neonate, which must be treated as a surgical emergency until proven otherwise
Abdominal tenderness, discoloration, or distension suggesting ischaemia or perforation
Signs of associated volvulus compromising bowel viability
Extensive atresia threatening inadequate residual bowel length
Rapid deterioration with sepsis or peritonitis
reference.prognosis: Isolated single atresias repaired promptly have excellent outcomes, whereas apple-peel and multiple atresias, or those complicated by extensive bowel loss, may lead to short-bowel syndrome and prolonged parenteral nutrition dependence. Overall survival with modern neonatal surgical and nutritional care is high.
pitfalls: Delaying laparotomy in a neonate with bilious vomiting while awaiting non-urgent tests
Overlooking a second, more distal atresia at operation (multiple atresias)
Anastomosing grossly dilated proximal bowel without tapering, risking functional obstruction
Failing to measure remaining bowel length and anticipate nutritional needs
Attributing distal obstruction solely to atresia and missing coexisting cystic fibrosis
management: Stabilise preoperatively with nasogastric decompression, intravenous fluid resuscitation and correction of electrolyte disturbance
Resect the atretic segment with primary anastomosis, tapering or plicating dilated proximal bowel where needed
Assess and preserve bowel length at operation to anticipate short-bowel risk
Provide postoperative parenteral nutrition with graded introduction of enteral feeds as motility returns
Screen for cystic fibrosis and exclude coexisting malrotation given the overlapping presentations
Monitor nutrition long term and manage short-bowel syndrome in extensive, apple-peel or multiple atresias
Coordinate paediatric surgical, neonatal and dietetic multidisciplinary care
